scope: Du Bois's books to 1930, each in its first edition where an open scan was found: The Suppression of the African Slave-Trade (1896), The Philadelphia Negro (1899), The Souls of Black Folk (first edition, April 1903), John Brown (1909), The Quest of the Silver Fleece (1911), The Negro (1915), Darkwater (1920), The Gift of Black Folk (1924) and Dark Princess (1928), with Project Gutenberg transcriptions beside seven of them; The Conservation of Races (1897) and The Talented Tenth in The Negro Problem (1903), as transcriptions only; and the first number of The Crisis (November 1910), which he edited, in the facsimile of the Arno Press reprint (1969). His essay in The New Negro (1925) is seated in 26/02, with the anthology. QUEUED: the Atlanta University Publications he edited (1896–1914); The Horizon and The Moon; the further numbers of The Crisis to 1930; The Star of Ethiopia (1913); Africa, Its Place in Modern History (1930). Not seated: Black Reconstruction (1935) and everything after 1930, in copyright in the United States.

why_seated: MANUS, 27 October 2026, after the twenty-fourth seating set the Book of Mormon on the shelf ("its as american as literature comes. but then i am like, i dont have king of malcolm or mao. it leads down a path where things start getting hairy"): "du bois and langston hughes are public domain tho, right?" — then "lets seat what can be seated of du bois and hughes", and, versioning the originals packet to include them: "the canon's america is way too white". The shelf held America in Whitman, Dickinson, Pound, Stein, the Book of Mormon and the Millerites; Du Bois is seated as far as the public domain reaches, and with him the first number of the magazine in which Hughes's first poem appeared.
ruling: Seated as far as the public domain reaches in the United States (published in 1930 or earlier), in English, the language they wrote in; first editions where an open scan was found, transcriptions named as transcriptions (MANUS, 2026-10-27).
